description: We are a team of six second-semester Computer Science students at UNIFAGOC, brought together by curiosity, a passion for technology, and a desire to turn ideas into solutions. We are participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge to apply our knowledge, explore new challenges, and learn as a team. We believe that collaboration, creativity, and dedication are essential to developing solutions that benefit society and deepen our understanding of the world and the universe.
summary:
We built Apollo6 for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to show what astronauts have to deal with inside a spacecraft on the way to the Moon and back. It is a 3D game made in Godot and follows a fictional mission inspired by Apollo 11. Before launch, you choose a science objective and decide how much food, water, equipment, and backup supplies to bring. Every item takes up storage space and adds mass, so what you pack affects what you can do later.

Once in flight, you move through the cabin in first person, pushing off surfaces and drifting in microgravity. Across five playable days, hunger and thirst keep rising while you follow checklists and handle problems like power alerts and life-support issues. You secure floating objects, fill a drinking pouch, and realign the high-gain antenna to restore contact with Houston. You also replace a carbon dioxide scrubber cartridge, showing how keeping the cabin habitable can become as urgent as staying on course.

Along the way, you carry out the translunar injection burn, correct your trajectory, and control the lunar module's descent while watching your speed, attitude, and propellant. On the Moon, you collect a sample, deploy a laser retroreflector, or take stereo photographs of the regolith, depending on what you packed. On the way back, you deploy the main parachutes during Earth reentry. After a safe splashdown, the mission report shows how your choices affected crew survival, spacecraft systems, and the mission's scientific results.
details:
Apollo6 Project Details

We built Apollo6 to show what astronauts have to deal with inside a spacecraft on the way to the Moon and back. In this first-person 3D game, you fly a fictional mission inspired by Apollo 11 and make the decisions that keep the crew going.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Apollo6 main menu showing the lunar module and Earth above the Moon." ]

The Apollo6 main menu, with the lunar module on the surface and Earth in the distance.

What We Want Players to Learn

We wanted players to see how much work happens between launch and landing. In a cramped cabin, even filling a drinking pouch or putting equipment away takes care. We want players to understand why astronauts use checklists and plan reserves before they need them. In the game, you find out what happens when several tasks need your attention at once.

How the Game Works

Before launch, you choose a lunar science objective and pack the instrument it requires. Food, water, tools, and backup equipment all compete for limited storage and add mass. A spare battery can help during a power spike. You still need enough rations to cover five playable days and three mission transitions.

From Earth Orbit to the Moon

Getting to the Moon starts with translunar injection, the engine burn that sends the spacecraft out of Earth orbit toward the Moon. You correct the trajectory as needed, then control the lunar module's descent by managing thrust, tilt, and touchdown speed.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The S-IVB third stage fires above Earth as the player monitors the translunar injection guidance display." ]

The Saturn V third stage fires during translunar injection.

Life Inside the Spacecraft

You push off from surfaces and drift through the cabin in microgravity. While keeping track of food and water, you follow the day's checklist, secure loose objects, and realign the high-gain antenna to restore contact with Houston.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"First-person view of the Apollo6 command console with flight instruments and the daily checklist." ]

The command console on the outbound trip. The HUD tracks the day's tasks, supplies, hunger, and thirst.

Keeping the Air Breathable

One checklist task is replacing a lithium hydroxide canister that removes carbon dioxide from cabin air. You open the compartment, remove the used canister, and align the replacement with its guides before seating it.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"Life-support minigame showing the replacement carbon dioxide scrubber cartridge and its alignment control." ]

The life-support station during the replacement canister's alignment step.

Science on the Surface

On the Moon, use the instrument you packed to collect a rock sample, deploy a laser retroreflector for Earth–Moon ranging, or take stereo photographs of the lunar soil.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"A flag stands beside the lunar module in Apollo6 after the laser retroreflector activity." ]

The flag goes up after the lunar laser-ranging activity records a return signal.

The Return to Earth

On the way home, you correct your trajectory and deploy Columbia’s three main parachutes during reentry. After splashdown, the report shows how your choices affected the crew, spacecraft, and science.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The Columbia command module descends toward the ocean below three open orange-and-white main parachutes." ]

Columbia descends under its three main parachutes before splashdown.

Tools and Technologies

We built Apollo6 in Godot 4 with GDScript and used Blender to model the command console, lunar module, and lunar terrain.

Data Sources

NASA Apollo mission records and technical reports. We used the Apollo 11 mission timeline to structure Apollo6, from translunar injection and lunar landing to Columbia's return to Earth. NASA's recorded injection speed of about 10.83 km/s set the target for the engine-burn challenge, and the recorded parachute deployment altitudes informed the timing challenge during reentry. We used NASA's crew stowage report to design a cabin task in which players secure loose equipment in microgravity. NASA's science reports also informed three lunar activities. Players can collect rock samples, take stereo photographs of the lunar soil, or place a retroreflector to show how a laser pulse sent from Earth can be used to measure the distance to the Moon. We compressed the mission timeline and simplified the procedures for gameplay.
